history.title: Take It Apart

data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Most bad arguments are not lies. They are true facts stapled to a claim they do not actually support. This week you learn to spot the gap, and to stop leaving one in your own writing.

1. Read **Says Who?**
2. Learn the words in **Argument Words**, then win the **Crossword** and the **Matching** game.
3. Keep the **Three Parts, Two Gaps** chart open while you read anything.
4. Trace **How an Argument Holds Together** before the quiz.
5. Sort the cards in **Claim, Evidence, or Reasoning?**
6. Use the **Argument Frames** out loud before you write.
7. Take **Argument Check**.
8. Lock it in with **Remember the Three Parts**.
9. Read **Argument Questions Kids Ask**.
10. Finish with **Decide: Which Argument Should the School Act On?**

Your job this week: find one real argument — an advert, a headline, a group chat — and name its three parts, or say which one is missing. 🧩

Picture panels: A claim and its support; Connect evidence to a conclusion; Check what is missing; Evaluate another proposal. Pictures support interpretation of the editable lesson text; they are not standalone evidence or answer keys. Numerical records and named practice stories are fictional. Read each sort in its stated context. Educator review is pending.

Sort by each sentence’s stated role in the three fictional proposals. All numbers here are invented classroom data. An evidence statement can also be a factual assertion outside its supporting role.

history.title: Says Who?
history.data:
## Says Who?

“We should keep the library open until five.” This is a **claim**: a statement the writer wants us to accept. It recommends a policy. A claim can also concern a checkable fact, such as the library's current closing time. Facts and claims are not opposites.

An **argument** offers support for a claim. Claim, evidence and reasoning form a useful classroom model, though real arguments can be organized in many ways. **Evidence** is information offered as support: observations, records, examples or accurate quotations. **Reasoning** explains why that information bears on the claim and how far the conclusion can go.

Consider this invented example. A school has 120 students in its year group. During one week, its librarian records 40 different students using the library after three. Those are fictional records for practice, not research findings. A writer argues that keeping the library open later could meet an existing need for after-school access: 40 is one third of 120. That explains a connection, but it does not show that all 40 want to stay until five or that staffing costs are covered. More information is needed.

Now try another invented example. Six of eleven team members report a fixed commitment on Tuesdays. This is relevant to a proposal to move practice, because a time when many cannot attend limits participation. It does not establish that Thursday is better: check Thursday availability and other constraints too. Reasoning helps interpret evidence; reasoning alone cannot replace missing evidence.

A **counterclaim** opposes a claim. An objection may also challenge the evidence or reasoning. State a strong, relevant objection fairly rather than making it easy to dismiss. A **rebuttal** responds with reasons and evidence; it can also acknowledge a real limitation or revise the original proposal.

A **fact** is something that is the case and can be checked with appropriate evidence. A factual assertion still needs verification. An **opinion** is a judgment or belief, sometimes a personal preference. Opinions about what a school should do can be supported and debated; they are not automatically worthless or beyond reasoning.

Evidence is **relevant** if it bears on the particular claim. Reliable information about the color of the library walls would not settle its opening hours. Check the **source**, the way information was gathered, alternative explanations and the limits of the conclusion. Apply these questions even to arguments whose conclusions you already like.

For the sort, use the assigned role in three fictional proposal contexts: library access, cooking practice, and team scheduling. An evidence statement is itself an assertion, but in these arguments it serves as support. Read the wording and role, not just the picture.

history.meta: 6 frames • say them out loud before writing • rubric included

items.text: The evidence offered is ____, which came from ____.

data.rubric:
| Criteria | 1 — Starting | 3 — Getting There | 5 — Evaluator |
|---|---|---|---|
| Finding the parts | Names the topic | Names claim and evidence | Names claim, evidence and reasoning, and quotes each |

history.title: Argument Check

questions.question: Fictional argument: “Keep the library open until five. Forty students used it after three.” What is missing?
options: An explanation connecting current use to the proposed hours, including limits
A claim of any kind
Any information offered as support
Nothing; the ideal closing time has been established
questions.correctAnswer: An explanation connecting current use to the proposed hours, including limits

questions.question: Which statement proposes an action rather than asserting a current fact?
options: The posted opening time is 8:15
The school should open its library an hour later in the afternoon
The attendance record lists 62 visits
The timetable lists a bus arrival at 7:52
questions.correctAnswer: The school should open its library an hour later in the afternoon

questions.question: What does it mean for evidence to be relevant?
options: It comes from a source that is recent and well known
It is interesting enough to keep the reader's attention
It bears on this particular claim, not just the topic
It is a number rather than a story or a quotation
questions.correctAnswer: It bears on this particular claim, not just the topic

questions.question: What can a well-supported response to a relevant counterclaim do?
options: Guarantee that everyone agrees
Replace the need for evidence
Show how the argument handles a serious objection or limit
Prove that opposing views are always false
questions.correctAnswer: Show how the argument handles a serious objection or limit

questions.question: Which is the most thorough way to evaluate support?
options: Trust a familiar source without checking
Check relevance, source quality, reasoning and alternative explanations
Count pieces of evidence only
Accept evidence placed near the beginning
questions.correctAnswer: Check relevance, source quality, reasoning and alternative explanations

questions.question: Fictional argument: “We should ban phones at lunch. Our survey reports increased phone use.” Identify the claim and offered evidence, and explain what still needs checking.
questions.expectedAnswer: The claim recommends a lunchtime ban. The offered evidence is a reported increase in use. Check the survey and whether it concerns lunch, explain the claimed problem, and evaluate evidence about the proposed response. An increase alone does not establish that a ban would help.

questions.question: Write a claim you agree with, then state the strongest objection to it as fairly as you can.
questions.expectedAnswer: Answers vary. A full answer states an arguable claim, then gives an objection a thoughtful opponent would actually make, phrased without mockery or a weakened version, showing the student can represent the other side accurately.

reflections.text: What is an argument you have heard recently that had evidence but no reasoning?
Was it harder to state the objection fairly than you expected? Why?

history.title: Argument Questions Kids Ask

data.question: Is an opinion just a weak claim? 🤔
data.answer: Opinions include judgments and beliefs as well as preferences. An opinion about a policy can be supported with reasons. Claims can concern facts, values or actions; these categories do not make facts and claims opposites.

data.question: Can evidence be true and still be bad evidence?
data.answer: Yes. A true detail can be irrelevant to the particular conclusion. Also check whether a purported fact is actually verified.

data.question: Does more evidence always make an argument stronger? 📊
data.answer: No. Quality, relevance, sufficiency and the explanation matter. More weak evidence does not automatically overcome a gap.

data.question: What if I cannot find a counterclaim?
data.answer: Check whether there is a serious opposing claim, alternative explanation or limitation. Do not invent a false balance where evidence strongly supports one conclusion.

data.question: Is it fine to argue for something I do not believe? 🎭
data.answer: A classroom exercise can ask you to examine another position. Represent it honestly, distinguish the exercise from your own belief, and avoid making up support.

data.question: Do adults get this wrong too?
data.answer: People of any age can overlook weak reasoning. Evaluate specific examples fairly rather than assuming an entire kind of writing is unreliable.

history.title: Decide: Which Argument Should the School Act On?
history.meta: 6th Grade • Decision brief • judge the arguing, not the outcome

data.title: Which Argument Should the School Act On?
data.instructions: Four groups want the same money. Judge the arguments, not the causes. Recommend one, and be able to say why the best-argued case was not necessarily the one you liked.
data.fitReason: RI.6.8 asks students to distinguish claims supported by reasons and evidence from claims that are not. Forcing a single recommendation from four proposals makes that distinction consequential instead of an exercise.

brief.context:
Classroom simulation: one equal-sized grant can support one proposal. All records below are invented. Compare the quality of these short arguments; a real funding decision would need verified costs and fuller information.
A. Library: Extend opening to five for a trial. A fictional log records 40 of 120 students after three in one week. That suggests demand for access, but a trial should record later-hour demand and staffing costs before permanent expansion.
B. Sports: Buy new equipment. A fictional record lists 50 club members. That proves new equipment is the best use of the grant.
C. Cooking: Offer a trial club. In a fictional survey, 19 of 28 respondents said they would join. Interest supports exploring a club, but actual attendance, accessible facilities, supervision and costs need checking.
D. Rehearsal: Fund an extra rehearsal session. Music is the best activity, so everyone will benefit.
Recommend which case is best supported as written, acknowledge missing information, and distinguish this from deciding the final real-world budget.
brief.audience: A simulated school panel that needs a reasoned recommendation
brief.drivingQuestion: Which of these four proposals is the best argued, and is that the same as the one you would most like to see happen?
brief.seedDirection: Score the arguing before you notice which cause you prefer. Write the claim, evidence and reasoning of each proposal down before forming any view.
lockedLessonFacts: Claims can concern facts, values or proposed actions.
Evidence must be relevant, reliable and sufficient for the conclusion.
Reasoning explains the link and its limitations.
A counterclaim is an opposing claim, and a rebuttal responds.
openQuestions: Which proposal has evidence that would fit a different conclusion equally well?
Does any proposal name the strongest objection to itself?
Where does your own preference sit, and did it affect your scoring?
stakeholders: The four groups who wrote the proposals
Students who benefit from whichever wins
criteria: Identify claim, evidence and reasoning for all four proposals; explicitly mark a missing part
Each proposal is rated for reasoning and for whether it handles a counterclaim
One recommendation, with the reason stated in terms of the arguing
An honest sentence saying whether your preferred cause was also the best argued
At least four glossary words used correctly
constraints: Judge the argument as written, not what the group meant
Quote a supporting line for each rating, or state that the required support is absent
brief.deliverable: A panel report: a table of the four proposals broken into claim, evidence and reasoning, a rating for each, one recommendation with its reason, and one sentence about your own preference.

parallelExample.context: Invented example: a panel initially prefers the sports proposal.
parallelExample.move: The panel notices that participation alone does not establish an equipment need. It compares the library and cooking proposals’ explanations and limitations before making a provisional recommendation.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: They separated the quality of the case from the appeal of the cause, which is what the panel was actually asked to judge.
